Yale SOM · MGT 409 AI Foundations for Managers · Fall 2026 · Final project (solo)

Anvaya · अन्वय

Understand the policies shaping India. Indian laws and policy documents are public but written in dense, archaic legal language that most citizens cannot read. Anvaya is an independent, evidence-first assistant that finds the official documents, explains in plain language how a policy affects the reader, and shows the exact passage behind every claim.

Anvaya answers one kind of question: what does this law say, is it in force, and what does it mean for me? A reader can ask for any bill or Act by name, or paste a link to an official document. A verification engine searches Parliament’s register and India Code, downloads every official version, runs a list of explicit checks (shown to the reader, each with its source), and only then explains the document in plain language, with each statement tied to a verbatim quote and page of the official text. Legal status is computed from the Gazette dates by code, and AI is used only to explain a document and to answer a reader’s own questions from retrieved official text, with a second AI pass that checks each sentence. 22 bills and Acts are already in the register. One of them, India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, was reviewed claim by claim and is used throughout this report as a worked example, because it is being switched on in three steps (13 November 2025, 13 November 2026, 13 May 2027) and shows why status has to be computed.

154/154evidence quotes found on the stated page of the official PDF (checked 2026-10-25)
21/25 · 10/10strict-assertion pass, development set · held-out set (model gpt-6-luna)
6/6indirect prompt-injection attacks resisted; none cited
126 + 38unit tests + browser tests on a production build, all passing, including the live-model tests

2. Motivation

Who has this problem?

Anyone a law applies to who is not a lawyer. Indian Acts, rules and Gazette notifications are public, but they are written in a drafting style ordinary citizens cannot read: very long sentences, nested cross-references to other Acts, amendments written as substitutions (“for the word X, substitute Y”), and the real detail deferred to rules “as may be prescribed”. A shopkeeper who holds customer data, a student, a gig worker or a journalist is governed by these texts but rarely reads them.

UserQuestionWhat Anvaya gives
Citizen or studentWhat is this law and does it affect me?A short brief, what changes, who is affected, source one click away
Small-business ownerWhat must I do, and by when?Duties with their start dates, an explicit “no automatic small-business exemption”, no invented cost figure
Journalist or civic groupWhat actually passed, and what changed since?Dated legal journey; things we could not confirm are listed
Researcher or analystIs the claim in this article true?Exact passage and PDF page for each statement; abstention when the text is silent

How do they cope today, and what does it cost?

They read press summaries, ask a friend, accountant or lawyer, try to read the Gazette PDFs, or ask a chatbot. The costs:

  • Time. The DPDP Act alone is 10,722 words, about 54 min to read once at 200 words a minute (legal text reads slower). The six documents that together decide what applies and when are 23,308 words, about 1 h 57 min. The word counts are measured; the reading speed is an assumption.
  • Money. Paying a professional to explain a law is the alternative to reading it. We did not measure what that costs, so we claim no figure.
  • Frustration and risk. The answer to “does this apply to me?” depends on several documents with different start dates, and secondary sources disagree on the exact day. A person who guesses wrong either complies too early or misses a duty. A general chatbot, asked the same questions, failed most of our strict fact checks (section 3).

Example. A small-business owner asks: “Does the DPDP Act apply to me, and when?” The honest answer needs five official documents that sit in separate Gazette PDFs: the Act (assented 11 August 2023), a commencement notification (13 November 2025) that switches on different sections on three different dates, the Rules (13 November 2025) with their own three-date schedule, a corrigendum to the Rules (11 December 2025), and a Removal of Difficulties Order (published 6 October 2026, nineteen days before this report). While building Anvaya the first version of the app held three of these. Searching the web also showed that secondary sources disagree on the exact day the main duties start (13 or 14 May 2027) and that the press reported, without any official notification, that the Government might shorten the 18-month wait. A reader cannot sort that out without reading Gazette PDFs.

How hard is the text? Measured on the documents in the register. Using the Flesch–Kincaid grade formula (a rough proxy for reading difficulty, not a comprehension test) on the 17 stored documents with at least 100 sentences:

Median sentence length (words)Flesch–Kincaid grade
Official text (17 documents, grades 13.9–28.4)42.921.4
Anvaya’s plain-language briefs and change summaries (22 documents)18.714.3

Two honest readings. The difficulty is mostly structure, not old words: archaic terms such as “notwithstanding” and “thereof” appear only about 2.2 times per 1,000 words, while 1.7 per 1,000 words defer detail to later rules or notifications that a reader cannot see in the Act. And Anvaya’s text is about 2.3 times shorter-sentenced but still college-level on this formula: clearer, not yet plain. We did not test comprehension with readers.

Why should anyone care?

Laws bind people whether or not they can read them. A policy that cannot be read cannot be questioned, complied with or held to account, and a citizen who cannot check a claim must trust whoever tells them. Making the text legible, with the original one click away so the explanation can be checked, lets people see for themselves how a policy affects them. That is the whole aim of the project.

Where this project started

An earlier build of Anvaya was functional but failed the user. Its “30-second brief” described the app’s own import process instead of the law, internal values such as effective_on_schedule were shown to readers, an “Analyze stakeholders” button produced only “analysis completed”, and unrelated inflation data was advertised on a data-protection page. The rebuild described here changed the product contract, not just the styling.

3. What Is New

What already exists

ProductWhat it does wellWhat it does not do for this problem
ChatGPT and similar chatbotsFluent explanations of almost anything, instantly; can browse the web.Not limited to the official text and not checked against it; no page-level citation of the Gazette by default; recent notifications may be missing. Measured below with the same model as Anvaya.
Google SearchFinds pages quickly.Returns pages, not an answer; the reader still has to read and interpret the law.
India Code (Legislative Department)The authoritative statute book for central Acts.Organised by document and written in the original language of the Act; no plain-language explanation; many amending Acts are not listed.
Digital Sansad (Parliament)Official register and texts of bills and their stages.No explanation; each version is a separate PDF. Anvaya uses it as a source and checks it.
PRS Legislative ResearchExpert-written summaries and trackers for selected bills.Not question-driven and covers selected bills only; written by hand, so it cannot cover every document on demand.
Indian KanoonFree search over Indian statutes and judgments.A search engine over documents: it finds text but does not explain what a policy means for a person.

These descriptions are of how each product is generally used; we did not benchmark them. Only the chatbot comparison below is measured.

What Anvaya does differently

IdeaWhat Anvaya does
Evidence at claim levelFor the worked example (DPDP), 83 claims each carry verbatim quotes and a PDF page; a script found 154 of 154 quotes on the stated page. A fabricated quote or the wrong page fails the test.
Status computed, not generatedStart dates come from the Gazette notification; code computes “in force / starts in 200 days” from today’s date. The Act and the Rules have separate schedules. AI cannot write status.
A verification engineFor a name, search Parliament’s register and India Code, download every official version, and run explicit checks (the register’s stage, the documents’ own printed title, Bill number, assent date and Act number, India Code’s record, the Gazette copy). Each check is shown with its source. 5 of 22 stored records are corroborated by a second official source, 0 failed. It uses no AI.
Answer, then checkRetrieval is scoped to one policy. The model must cite passage IDs and may abstain. A second call judges each sentence against its passages; code confirms each quote appears word for word. The result is shown to the reader.
A scorecard, with its uncertaintyFour rings score how a law is built (clarity, enforceability, proportionality, accountability) by formula from the official text, each with a 90% range and a click-through comparison with 18 UK and Canadian statutes. A fifth ring, evidence of effect, is deliberately blank: no outcome data exists, so Anvaya refuses to infer one.
Uncertainty as a featureA “Things to watch” section lists what could not be confirmed, with sources labelled official or secondary. Points that are our interpretation are marked “Our reading, not the law”.

An honest comparison, measured

To isolate what retrieval and checking add, we asked the same model (gpt-6-luna) the 29 answerable benchmark questions with no documents and no checks, the way a general chatbot answers from memory, and scored both with the same strict assertions.

SystemStrict pass (of 29)Comment
Plain chatbot: same model, no documents61 question was blocked by the provider’s content filter and counted as a miss. Failures were mostly the start dates (13 November 2026, 13 May 2027), the October 2026 Removal of Difficulties Order and section numbers; it cites no pages.
Anvaya: retrieval, answer, second-pass check25The 4 misses are correct answers worded unexpectedly (disclosed in section 7).

Read this carefully. This is not a test of ChatGPT itself: ChatGPT can browse the web and may do better on recent facts, and we had no access to it on the course key, so we did not test it. The assertions are strict patterns written for the official wording, which penalises a correct answer in other words; that applies to both rows. Where others are better: India Code is the authority on the text, PRS summaries are written by experts and may be more nuanced than ours, and Anvaya depends on both Parliament’s and India Code’s data.

Scope, honestly. One law (DPDP) is hand-reviewed claim by claim. 22 further bills and Acts from Parliament’s register are verified by the engine against official sources, which is a lower standard: the checks prove identity, stage and dates, not that a plain-language reading is right. Anvaya is not legal advice and not an official service. The scorecard describes how a law is built and does not measure whether it works; the Economic Evidence Lab shows general official statistics, is labelled a future feature, and is not tied to any law.

4. The Agents

The agents are scoped roles in a fixed pipeline, not free-roaming tool users. The model never fetches anything or chooses tools; all retrieval and network access is done by code. That choice is deliberate: it keeps the set of things the model can influence small and testable.

RoleWhat it doesTools and calls
Resolver (code)Matches a question to one of 9 prepared answers (each cites verified quotes, no AI) or sends it on.Token overlap ≥ 0.8; answer expires on a date if it would become stale
Retrieval (code)Ranks passages from this policy only: BM25 with a legal-vocabulary synonym map, plus passages that contain the evidence of the best-matching reviewed claims, plus the claim notes themselves.Six official PDFs plus reviewed claim notes; code in lib/ask/retrieval.ts
Answer agentWrites 1–4 statements, each with the passage IDs that support it, or abstains. Receives a STATUS block computed by code.Portkey Responses API, gpt-6-luna, 1 call
Verification agentJudges each statement supported / partly / unsupported against its cited text. Unsupported details are dropped; an unsupported headline answer becomes an abstention.Same API, 1 call
Resolver and verification engine (code)Searches Parliament’s register and India Code, ranks matches, fetches every official version, and runs the checks. No model is involved, so verification costs no tokens and cannot be talked into anything.Sansad getBills; India Code (DSpace API); HTTPS fetch to allowlisted hosts; PDF text extraction; SQLite
Scoring engine (code)Reads the stored official text, flags provisions with phrase patterns tied to the literature, computes 17 bounded indicators in four dimensions, resamples for a 90% range, and benchmarks against fetched UK and Canadian statutes. Estimators for an “effect” ring (difference-in-differences, interrupted time series, synthetic control, meta-analysis) exist but are gated off until real outcome data is loaded.No model, no tokens. lib/scoring/; comparators fetched once by scripts/build-benchmarks.ts
Analysis agentFor a retrieved document, selects up to 14 passages with eight fixed retrieval probes (purpose, definitions, duties, penalties, bodies, application, rights, exemptions) and writes a brief, 3–5 changes and 2–4 affected groups, each with passage IDs. Then the verification agent checks every statement; unsupported ones are dropped. The result is cached.Same API, 2 calls per document, once

Models used, and why

Every model call uses gpt-6-luna through the course Portkey key, for three jobs: the answer agent, the verification agent and the analysis agent. The reasons are practical. It is the only model the course key allows, and it is a single model on purpose, so cost and behaviour are predictable and every number in this report refers to one model. Everything that does not need judgment (matching a question to a prepared answer, retrieval, status, fetching, verification of a bill, scoring) is ordinary code, which costs nothing, is deterministic and cannot be talked into anything. An earlier model (gpt-5.6-luna) was also benchmarked and gave a similar cost profile; the code reads ANVAYA_MODEL, so a different model can be tried with one setting.

One real run, step by step

Question: “Do I have to ask customers for permission before sending them promotional emails under this Act?” on the DPDP page. Figure 4a shows this question in the app; the table is the logged trace of a second run of it (data/benchmarks/trace-run.json, written by scripts/trace-run.ts from the real pipeline and the agent log).

The verification call’s tokens are the totals minus the answer call, because the log records the answer call separately. This run was a repeat of a question asked minutes earlier, which is why most of its input tokens were cached (section 5).

Engine traces. Searching “Taxation bill” matched several bills and offered the alternatives instead of silently choosing. “The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026” resolved to Lok Sabha Bill No. 150 of 2026, enacted as Act No. 21 of 2026: Parliament’s record, the printed “assented to on 17 AUG 2026, Act No. 21 of 2026” on the passed text, and the dates in each House all agreed, while India Code did not yet list the Act and the page says so. A name that matches nothing (“zzz flibbertigibbet statute”) produced no record. Pasting the January 2025 draft DPDP Rules link (a document the app had never seen) fetched a 51-page bilingual PDF, titled it from its own short-title clause, labelled it “draft published for public comment”, and produced a checked analysis (a brief, 5 changes and 4 affected groups; 10 of 14 statements fully supported).

5. Tokenomics

Tokens per run, measured from real runs

MeasurementRunsInput per runof which cachedOutput per run
Benchmark: 25 development + 10 held-out questions, gateway cache bypassed (31 full answers, two calls each; the rest abstained after one)354,337not recorded then896
Fresh check on 26 Oct: 10 different questions, cached tokens recorded104,1600 (0%)758
The traced question, repeated minutes after the same question was asked (section 4)14,6033,225 (70%)1,062

A typical live run is therefore two model calls, about 4,337 input and 896 output tokens, and a median of 8 s (90th percentile 12.9 s). Cached input tokens appear only when the same prompt prefix was sent shortly before: none in 10 different questions, 70% on a repeat. The app shows these numbers under every live answer (Figure 4a), and the agent log (data/logs/agent-executions.jsonl, 680 rows) records them. The 9 prepared answers cost zero tokens. Verifying a bill record and computing a scorecard use no model.

Analysis of a retrieved document costs one writing call and one checking call, once, because the result is stored. Across 46 logged writing calls the mean was about 4,495 input and 3,510 output tokens; the checking call was not logged separately, so the true total is higher.

Cost per run, per user per month, and at 100 and 10,000 users

Price. Cost is tokens times the provider’s rate. This project uses the course Portkey key and we could not verify a public price for gpt-6-luna, so we claim no real dollar cost. The table shows how cost scales using three illustrative rate pairs (input / output, dollars per million tokens), so a reader can substitute the real rate. We also assume 20 live questions per user per month; that is an assumption, not measured usage, and cached-token discounts and hosting are not included.

Illustrative rate in / outPer runPer user per month100 users10,000 users
$0.50 / $2.00$0.0040$0.08$8$792
$2.00 / $8.00$0.0158$0.32$32$3,168
$5.00 / $20.00$0.0396$0.79$79$7,921

In tokens, which do not depend on price: 100 users at 20 questions each is 2,000 live runs a month (8.7M input, 1.8M output tokens); 10,000 users is 200,000 runs (867.4M input, 179.2M output). Prepared answers and caching would reduce this, so these are upper estimates for the stated usage.

What we did to keep cost down, and whether quality suffered

MeasureEffect on tokensEffect on quality (evidence)
Prepared answers for the most common questionsZero tokens, instant.No loss: each cites quotes verified against the PDFs; each expires on a date so it cannot go stale silently.
Retrieve 8 passages instead of sending the whole corpusThe six official documents are about 23,308 words, roughly 31,077 tokens; a question sends about 4,337, 86% less.A real cost: retrieval found a page containing the answer for 18/18 development and 6/8 held-out questions that have one, so some questions can be answered from the wrong passages (a paraphrase was one such miss).
Cache answers (by policy, question, document version, model, date) and analyses (stored once per document)A repeat of a question reuses the stored answer; the provider cached 70% of input tokens on the repeat we measured.No measured loss; the cache key includes the document version and date so a changed document is not served a stale answer.
Do verification, scoring and fetching in codeNo tokens for any of them.Better, not worse: deterministic and testable (126 unit tests).
Output caps and a bounded retryReplies are capped (2,400 tokens, one retry at 5,000), so a runaway reply cannot spend without limit.One failure mode seen earlier: a long reply was cut off and unreadable; the retry with a larger cap fixed it.
A cost we chose not to cut: the second-pass checkIn the traced run it added 1,375 input and 316 output tokens (30% and 30% of the run) and a second call.It earns its cost: over the benchmarks it checked 76 statements and found 73 fully supported; the rest were flagged or dropped before display. Requiring exact quotes raised output tokens 25% and median latency from 6.5 s to 8 s. We did not run a without-check ablation, and we did not test a cheaper model, so there is no measured quality-per-dollar comparison between models.

6. Safety

Retrieved documents, web pages and questions are treated as untrusted input. The table lists each risk, what protects against it, and the evidence we have. All results are from the saved test outputs; the samples are small and were written by us.

RiskDefenceEvidence
Fetching an attacker’s or internal address (SSRF)Official sites only, HTTPS only, no IP addresses or credentials; every redirect is validated before it is requested; size and time limits.19 unit tests, including a redirect from an official host to 169.254.169.254, refused without being requested, and a redirect loop. This closed a gap in earlier code that checked only the final URL.
Wrong action: picking the wrong billA match must contain every distinctive word typed; generic words (“amendment”) only rank; a bill that became law beats a withdrawn one; ambiguous names show the alternatives.Unit tests per rule. Real defects fixed: “Waqf Amendment Bill 2025” once matched the Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill on the word “amendment”; an early stop returned a withdrawn bill.
Sources that disagree or cannot be readDisagreements are shown and graded (assent date and Act number fail a record; a passing date is reported). Unreadable PDFs are “could not check”, never “failed”.Found in real data and shown to the reader: a one-day disagreement on the Consumer Protection Bill’s Rajya Sabha date; an India Code enactment date that differs from Parliament’s; a PDF that extracts as gibberish.
Scores that look more certain than they areEvery score ships with a 90% range and a reason built from counts; a ratio with too little text is “not measurable”, never zero; there is no overall score; the effect ring stays blank without outcome data; a benchmark is refused for amending bills, rules and areas with no verified comparator.Unit tests for bounds, interval ordering, exact reproducibility, monotonicity and gating (tests/scoring.test.ts); the effect estimators recover known effects on simulated data (tests/outcomes.test.ts: difference-in-differences bias under 0.1 and near-nominal interval coverage over 150 simulations). A hand-read precision check of the phrase patterns found one (“reasonableness”) only about half right; it was tightened and everything re-scored.
Endless loops and runaway agentsThe pipeline is fixed: there is no model-driven loop and the model chooses no tools. Each question makes at most two model calls plus one bounded retry (a larger output cap, once); the client retries a failed request once and times out after 60 seconds (120 for an analysis). Duplicate requests for the same analysis share one in-flight job.The call counts are visible in every run: never more than 2 model calls in any of the 45 live questions measured (6 abstained after one call, 39 used two). Retry and cap constants are in lib/ask/answer.ts.
Overspending (a bug or a bad actor burning the token budget)Layers: per-client limit of 12 questions a minute; questions capped at 600 characters; output caps; answers and analyses cached; the analysis runs once per document; a daily token budget (default 2,000,000 tokens, ANVAYA_DAILY_TOKEN_BUDGET) after which live AI answers and new analyses pause while prepared answers, documents and verification keep working.4 unit tests for the budget (counting, tripping at the limit, daily reset, a refused question makes no model call). Figure 6b is the app with the budget set to 1 token: the first question is answered, the second is refused with a plain message. Limit: the counter lives in memory, so it resets if the server restarts, and the course key’s own limits are outside our control.
Instructions in the questionRules in the prompt; status block computed by code; output validated.“Ignore all previous instructions… fully in force”, a status-override request and a secrets request all failed to change the answer (benchmark cases a01, a04, a05; one browser test).
Instructions hidden in a retrieved document (indirect injection)Passages are delimited as data and the model is told never to obey them; cited IDs are validated; the second pass checks each sentence.6 poisoned passages added to a copy of the real corpus, each confirmed to reach the model: 6/6 ignored, 0 cited. n = 6, one run each.
Answers about the wrong lawOne corpus per policy; retrieval cannot cross it.DPDP question on the Waqf bill and on the Securities Code abstained (benchmark a03, holdout h10, browser test); no DPDP text appears on a researched bill’s page.
Fabricated citations or quotesPassage IDs must exist; unsupported statements dropped; quotes verified against the PDF.Verifier tests reject a made-up quote and a real quote on the wrong page. Second-pass result over the benchmarks: 73 of 76 statements fully supported; it also flagged overgeneralisations (for example “national interest” for named grounds).
Leaked secretsKeys read only on the server; .env ignored; logs hold no keys.The key value is absent from every file in the production build, the seed database, the reports and logs (scanned for the value itself).

Limits of this evidence. The checker is the same model family as the answerer, so errors can correlate. Six injection attacks are not a penetration test. Nothing here replaces review by a lawyer.

Answer quality (strict, mechanical assertions)

ModelSetStrict passNotes
gpt-6-luna (final)Development, 25 questions21/25Retrieval found a gold page in 18/18; 2 abstentions, all on questions built to be unanswerable or unsafe
gpt-6-luna (final)Held-out, 10 questions10/10Retrieval gold page 6/8; written after the last retrieval change, never tuned against
gpt-6-luna (before exact-quote checks)Development / held-out23/25 · 8/10Kept in data/benchmarks/archive/
gpt-5.6-luna (earlier)Development / held-out25/25 · 9/10Kept in data/benchmarks/archive/

Run-to-run variance is real: the held-out set scored 8/10 before the quote checks and 10/10 after, with no relevant change to retrieval, so single numbers should be read as ±2 questions. The 4 strict misses on the development set were each read by the developer and were substantively correct answers whose wording the pattern did not anticipate (for example “sections 1(2), 2, 18–26” where the pattern wanted a space around the dash, and “the purposes and means” where it wanted the singular); this is a reading by the developer, not independent review. The development set was used while building (one retrieval fix followed a failure, patterns were widened three times after correct answers), so its score is optimistic; the held-out set is the fairer figure. An earlier held-out run exposed a real weakness: a question about keeping data after withdrawing consent never retrieved the erasure passage (keyword retrieval missed the paraphrase), so the answer hedged. We did not tune against it.

Scorecard and engineering

  • All 23 register documents are scored; tiny amending bills come out “not enough evidence” in several dimensions instead of zero. Hand-read precision of the phrase patterns on one bill (nine random flagged sentences each): delegation 9 of 9, penalty size 9 of 9, deadlines 4 of 4; the reasonableness pattern was about half right and was tightened. Recall was not measured. The scores describe design, not whether a design works.
  • Across 22 stored analyses the second pass checked 272 statements: 241 fully supported, 31 marked “check the source”, 0 dropped before display.
  • A real defect surfaced and was fixed: the earlier ingestion labelled 3,500-character chunks as “pages”, so some page links were wrong. A second was found while taking Figure 4a: a quoted excerpt could begin mid-word, now trimmed and tested.
  • 126 unit tests and 38 browser tests on a production build pass; a clean copy with no key still serves every page and the prepared answers.

The missing evidence: a real user

The strongest evidence for this section would be a person trying the app, with a before-and-after time. We did not run one. A ready protocol is in docs/user-test-protocol.md: give 3–5 non-lawyers five questions about a law (for example “when must my business give a privacy notice?”), time how long it takes them with only the Gazette PDF and a search engine, then with Anvaya, and record whether their answers match the official text. Until that is done, the time figures above are estimates and the quality figures are our own tests.

Look and feel

The policy page answers “what is it, is it in force, what changes” in the first two screens, with one plain status and no internal values (a browser test asserts that no raw enum names appear). It also works on a phone.

8. Limits + Next Steps

Limits

  • One curated law. Only DPDP has hand-reviewed, claim-level content. The other 22 records are engine-verified: their stage and dates are checked, but nobody has read their explanations against the law.
  • Coverage. Name search covers Parliament’s bill register (bills, including those that became Acts) and India Code (Acts, central first). State-level material beyond India Code, rules, regulations and policies need a pasted link to an official document on an allowed site. Parliament’s register is the authority on a bill’s stage, so Anvaya cannot see anything Parliament has not recorded. India Code does not list many amending Acts, so a second-source confirmation is often unavailable. The eGazette, which sits behind a captcha, is not searched, so later notifications (including start dates) are not checked. Text shown for an Act is as published and may not merge later amendments.
  • Verified does not mean legally reviewed. “Verified” means the listed checks passed. It does not mean a lawyer has read the explanation. Scanned or legacy-font PDFs cannot be read or explained, and long documents are analysed from their 14 most relevant passages, so provisions can be missed.
  • Retrieval is keyword-based (BM25 plus a synonym map). Paraphrases can miss the right passage; the held-out set showed it.
  • Dates carry real uncertainty. The notification says “eighteen months from the date of publication”; we show 13 May 2027 and flag that some commentators count a day later. A reported proposal to shorten the wait is unconfirmed, from secondary sources. We could not read the eGazette directly to rule out a newer notification.
  • No independent review. Quote checks prove wording, not interpretation. The second-pass checker shares a model family with the answerer. No lawyer reviewed the content, and no user study was run.
  • The chatbot comparison is one model. It shows what retrieval and checking add for gpt-6-luna; it does not test ChatGPT itself or any other product, and its strict patterns penalise correct answers in other words.
  • The token budget is in memory and resets when the server restarts; a hosted version needs a shared counter.
  • Prices unverified, so cost is reported in tokens. The model is non-deterministic: repeated runs of the same set differed by one or two questions.
  • Out of scope today: news and public-debate analysis, alerts, Hindi, accounts, hosting, and any causal estimate of a law’s economic effect. The Evidence Lab is general MoSPI data, deliberately not tied to the Act.
  • Images. The homepage photographs of the new Parliament building come from an Architectural Digest India article and are credited, but they are not openly licensed; they are used at the author’s direction for a non-commercial course project and should be replaced or cleared before any wider use. The Wikimedia and government-licensed alternatives are in public/assets/.

Next steps

  1. Run the two-minute user test with 3–5 non-lawyers and publish the observations.
  2. Measure the scorecard’s phrase-matching recall on a hand-labelled set, add more comparator countries, and load real outcome studies so the effect ring can be switched on for a policy that has them.
  3. Read the eGazette (past its captcha) for notifications and start dates, merge amendments into Act text, and analyse long documents in sections.
  4. Add embedding-based retrieval next to BM25 and re-run the held-out set.
  5. Curate a second law end to end (the National Sports Governance Act is the natural candidate) using the same claim-and-quote contract.
  6. Have a lawyer review the claim registry; add review controls for correcting a summary without rewriting source text.
  7. Read the eGazette directly for amendments, and add a change monitor for the DPDP notifications.
  8. Add press coverage as attributed, source-linked context only if the sources and licensing allow it.
